intro: Click-to-Open Rate isolates how well an email's content and offer performed among the people who actually opened it. Enter clicks and opens to get the rate.

sections.heading: How CTOR is calculated
sections.body: CTOR = Clicks ÷ Opens — [the same unique-clicks-over-unique-opens shape ActiveCampaign uses to define Click-to-Open Rate](https://www.activecampaign.com/glossary/click-to-open-rate). Opens, not delivered emails, is the denominator: CTOR asks how the message performed among people who saw it, deliberately excluding everyone it reached but who never opened it at all.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 400 ÷ 2,500 = 16.00%. Of everyone who opened this email, 16% then clicked something inside it — a read on the content and offer itself, not on how many people the campaign reached in the first place.

sections.heading: Why CTOR can run above 100%
sections.body: Open tracking and click tracking work through different mechanisms: an open is typically registered by a tracking pixel loading, while a click is registered by following a link — and [many email clients block images, including tracking pixels, by default](https://glockapps.com/blog/why-email-open-rates-are-no-longer-a-reliable-metric/). That means a recipient can click a link inside an email whose pixel never loaded, so their click gets counted while their open never does. Clicks aren't guaranteed to be a subset of opens the way the formula might imply, which is why CTOR can occasionally read above 100% without anything being broken — it's a real signal about how open tracking missed someone, not a calculation error.

sections.heading: CTOR vs. Open Rate
sections.body: These sit right next to each other in the same funnel, but ask different questions with different denominators. [Open Rate](/calculators/open-rate) is opens over delivered — did the message get opened at all, out of everyone it reached. CTOR is clicks over opens — of the people who did open it, how many then engaged with what was inside. A campaign can have a weak open rate (a bad subject line, most of the list never opening) but a strong CTOR (the people who did open loved the content), or the reverse. Reading CTOR without knowing the open rate it's built on tells only half the story of how the campaign actually performed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Confusing CTOR with email CTR. CTOR divides by opens; [CTR](/calculators/ctr) as used in advertising divides by impressions, and email CTR (a related but distinct concept) divides by delivered — three different denominators answering three different questions.
Treating a CTOR above 100% as proof the tracking is broken. It's a real, explainable result when a recipient clicks without their open ever being registered, not evidence the numbers are wrong.
Reading CTOR in isolation without also checking open rate. A strong CTOR on a weak open rate still means most of the list never engaged at all — CTOR only describes the people who opened.

Comparing CTOR across campaigns with very different open rates without accounting for it. A campaign that only got opened by its most engaged subscribers will naturally post a higher CTOR than one opened broadly, for reasons that have nothing to do with the content quality being compared.

faq.a: Click-to-Open Rate (CTOR) is the percentage of email opens that resulted in a click, calculated as clicks divided by opens. Unlike open rate or email CTR, which both divide by everyone the message was delivered to, CTOR's denominator is only the people who actually opened the email — it's meant to isolate how well the content and offer performed once someone saw the message, separate from whether the message got opened in the first place. A CTOR of 16% means that of everyone who opened the email, 16% then clicked something inside it, independent of how many people the campaign reached overall.

Divide clicks by opens: CTOR = Clicks ÷ Opens. A campaign with 400 clicks from 2,500 opens has a CTOR of 400 ÷ 2,500 = 16.00%. Both numbers need to come from the same campaign and the same tracking window — clicks from a broader date range than the opens they're being divided by will overstate the rate. Most email platforms calculate and report CTOR automatically alongside open rate and email CTR, so it rarely needs to be computed by hand, but the formula matters for understanding exactly which population the resulting percentage describes and why it can move independently of open rate.

Because open tracking and click tracking rely on different mechanisms. An open is typically registered when a tracking pixel loads, but many email clients block images, including that pixel, by default. A click is registered separately, through a followed link, which doesn't depend on the pixel loading at all. That means a recipient can click a link inside an email whose open was never tracked, so their click counts toward the numerator while they never showed up in the denominator. It's an unusual result, not an error — it reflects a real gap in how opens get tracked, not a broken calculation.

faq.q: How is CTOR different from Open Rate?
faq.a: Open Rate divides opens by delivered emails — everyone the message reached, whether they opened it or not. CTOR divides clicks by opens — only the people who already opened the email, checking how many of them then clicked something inside it. A campaign can have a weak open rate but a strong CTOR if the people who did open it were highly engaged, or a strong open rate paired with a weak CTOR if the subject line worked but the content inside didn't land. Reading either number alone misses half the story; together they separate "did people open this" from "did the content work once they did."

There's no universal good CTOR — it depends on list quality, content type, and who actually opened the email in the first place, all of which shift the number for reasons unrelated to how compelling the content was. A campaign opened mostly by a small, highly engaged segment will naturally post a higher CTOR than one opened broadly by a less-engaged list, even with identical content inside. Rather than comparing against an outside number, CTOR is most useful tracked against your own send history for a similar audience and content type, since that comparison holds the open-quality variable roughly constant.

qaNotes: STANDARD depth (Batch 06). NEW runtime implementation - ctor was not previously live; added to calc-registry.ts (ctor: clicks/opens), calc-catalog.ts's LIVE_CALCULATOR_SLUGS, and test-calculators.mjs's own LIVE_SLUGS list. Formula/example independently verified: 400/2500=0.16=16.00%, matches calculator-catalog.json's exampleOutput exactly; independently re-tested with 2 additional valid cases (150/1000=15.00%, 0/500=0.00%) and edge cases (opens=0 -> NaN, matching the catalog's own documented edgeCase; clicks>opens -> a valid >100% result, not blocked - see next note) via the calc-registry.ts compute function directly. Metric-specific section (why-ctor-can-exceed-100) is the deliberate INVERSE of the open-rate.json correction pass in this same batch history: open-rate's numerator (opens) is a deduplicated, delivered-capped concept that cannot legitimately exceed 100%, so opens>delivered is now blocked at the runtime layer - but CTOR's numerator (clicks) and denominator (opens) are tracked through genuinely different mechanisms (pixel-load vs link-follow), so a click without a corresponding tracked open is a real, sourced, mechanically-explained phenomenon, not an artifact wrongly imported from a different metric's definition. No cross-field validation was added for ctor (clicks>opens is intentionally left uncapped, unlike open-rate) - this distinction is the actual research finding this section documents. Comparison-note (CTOR vs Open Rate) via numerator/denominator/business-question framing - written independently from open-rate.json's own 'open-rate-vs-ctor' comparison-note and ctr.json's own 'ctr-vs-ctor' comparison-note (no shared sentences with either). common-mistakes item 1 also disambiguates CTOR from the site's own advertising-context 'ctr' calculator (clicks/impressions) - a third denominator in the same naming family. External sources: ActiveCampaign's own CTOR definition (glossary page, same clicks/opens formula this calculator implements) and GlockApps (email deliverability platform, sourced specifically for 'many email clients block images including tracking pixels by default' - the mechanical fact behind the >100% edge case).
